reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose the root cause before replacing the converter: check for misfires, oil consumption, exhaust leaks, and a lazy/failed downstream O2 sensor (a bad rear sensor alone can mimic P0420). Replace the catalyst/manifold assembly with a CARB-compliant unit where required. For affected 2018 models verify VIN against emissions recall PC717 for a free repair. Average converter replacement is roughly $1,200-$1,850 depending on whether the integrated manifold assembly is needed.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Begin with a known-good OEM gas cap (aftermarket caps often will not seal). If the code persists, smoke-test the EVAP system; a sticking/leaking vent valve is the usual culprit and is replaced as a unit. OEM vent control valve part numbers for this generation include 14935-JF00E / 14935-JF01C / 14935-JF02C (supersession family 14935-JF00A through JF02C). Valve runs roughly $60-$110; OEM gas cap $25-$40.

Address related catalyst codes at the same time. On affected 2018 cars the manifold/catalyst was covered under emissions recall PC717.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Identify which actuator is clicking (air-mix vs. mode) and replace the failed unit. Part is inexpensive (~$30-$80); labor varies by location.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Inspect struts and strut mounts (also check sway-bar end links and control-arm bushings, which can mimic the same clunk). Replace front struts in matched pairs — loaded quick-strut assemblies simplify the job — and perform a four-wheel alignment afterward. OEM front strut part numbers for 2002-2006 include the 54302-xxxxx family (e.g., 54302-9E125); 2002-2007 use E4302-ZB03B-type members for some configurations. Quality complete strut assemblies are widely available aftermarket.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Confirm the bad coil by swapping the suspect coil to an adjacent cylinder and verifying the misfire follows it (e.g., P0301 becomes P0302). Replace the failed coil (OEM 22448-JA00C for 2007-2013, 22448-8H315-era for 2002-2006) and inspect coil boots and spark-plug wells for oil. If oil is present, replace the valve cover gasket / tube seals. Replace spark plugs at the same time; consider replacing all four coils on high-mileage cars. A new OEM coil runs roughly $30-$70 each.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose with a cold-start listen plus inspection of the front cover for guide debris. The fix is replacing the secondary timing chains, tensioner shoes/guide rails, and tensioners (and typically the primary chain components and oil seals) as a complete kit while the front cover is off. Per the Nissan secondary-chain TSB, key OEM parts are secondary chains 13028-ZK01C (x2) and tensioner-shoe/guide rails 13097-ZK01C (x2) plus o-rings/seals. Use OEM or quality kits; do all guides, tensioners, and chains together. It is 8-14 hours of labor due to front-cover access.

The fix is replacing the secondary timing chains, tensioner shoes/guide rails, and tensioners (and typically the primary chain components and oil seals) as a complete kit while the front cover is off. Per the Nissan secondary-chain TSB, key OEM parts are secondary chains 13028-ZK01C (x2) and tensioner-shoe/guide rails 13097-ZK01C (x2) plus o-rings/seals. Use OEM or quality kits; do all guides, tensioners, and chains together. It is 8-14 hours of labor due to front-cover access.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the brake system scanned for actuator/stroke-sensor fault codes. Confirm and replace the 12V battery first, since a weak 12V battery frequently mimics or triggers the fault. If the actuator itself is failing, the Intelligent Brake Unit / actuator assembly must be replaced and calibrated with Nissan Consult software. Some owners have had the stroke sensor replaced separately at lower cost. Parts are expensive and Nissan-quoted jobs commonly run $3,000-$4,000.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Have the brake system scanned for actuator/stroke-sensor fault codes. reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Get a four-wheel alignment and correct excessive front toe. Run tire pressure at the higher end of spec (many owners add a few psi over the door placard), rotate tires every 5,000-7,500 miles, and replace worn low-rolling-resistance OEM tires with higher-mileage rated tires (e.g., Michelin Energy Saver/Primacy). Regular rotation greatly evens out the front-vs-rear wear disparity.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Diagnose whether the PTC element itself has failed (often indicated by a blown HV PTC fuse). Replace the PTC heater assembly and the high-voltage fuse in the HV junction box. On 2011-2012 cars also check the coolant temperature sensor and coolant-heater relay/switching. Heat-pump-equipped trims (SV/SL) retain partial heat but still rely on the PTC for fast preheat/defrost in sub-freezing temps.

reviewedSourceEvidence.howToFix: Remove and thoroughly clean the throttle body/plate with throttle-body cleaner, then perform the mandatory Idle Air Volume Learning (idle relearn) procedure to prevent high/unstable idle. If cleaning doesn't resolve it, replace the electronic throttle body and relearn idle. Also inspect for vacuum leaks and a dirty MAF that can mimic the symptoms.
